context: a letter from F. T. Buckland, which you are answering
exchanges:
Will you allow me to call your attention to “Land & Water” a copy of which I now send you.

The Field behaved so badly to me that I simply withdrew from them—& I now conduct the portions of the paper to which my name is affixed—

The work I assure you is perfect slavery.

Will you kindly patronize me, & make my columns the medium for obtaining any information you require. I have a large staff of zoologists working for me at home, & a large correspondence abroad.

Trusting that you are much better in health

Yours ever | Most obedient & obliged | Frank Buckland

C Darwin Esq

I am much obliged for the Paper which is full of interesting matter and for your note. I am sure I should be very glad to be of any assistance to you but my health is too weak for me to offer to be a correspondent; nor do I think it likely that I should have any questions to ask, and so take advantage of your obliging offer. I am endeavouring to complete a book which has been many years on hand. Perhaps you may remember my asking you about the feet of otter hounds. You obtained some information but never sent it me, being I have no doubt so much pressed with other business. I now enclose a query on the same subject, if you will be so kind as to insert it; if you were to back it up with an editorial request my chance of answer would be better, though I am not sanguine. I have ordered from my news vendor “Land and Water” for the next six months.

With every good wish for your success and that your labour may grow lighter. | Believe me | Yours very faithfully | Charles Darwin
